A REFINERY SOLD FOR A RAND - WITH A LEGACY THAT WILL COST BILLIONS.

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We ask why two global oil companies - BP and Shell - have been able to away from a broken, non-functioning refinery, abandoning their responsibility to the community for decades of pollution, passing

Unique Selling Point:
We have access to whistleblower documents which show how consultants shifted their perspective from one year to the next on why selling the SAPREF refinery in Durban was a good idea for government. Those whistleblower documents suggest that behind the wall of silence on the sale in which the state paid a single rand there may have been manipulation to tie South Africa back in to a fossil fuel agenda.

Summary:
• In May 2024, the state-owned Central Energy Fund (CEF) agreed to acquire the SAPREF refinery assets in South Durban from BP and Shell for R1 (symbolic sum), subject to approvals, after it had been flooded in 2022.
• A whistle-blower dumped 1000 + pages of documents at OUTA including complicated Due Diligence documents, suggesting that government was taking this decision without proper advice or advice designed to avoid the questions of environmental liability.
• Open Secrets then published whistle-blower-backed investigations (July 2025) detailing the R1 sale and the “clean-break/voetstoots” nature of the deal and due-diligence red flags.
• One of the red flags is concern about the role of a consulting company Centurion Law Group which has a known poor track record in advising Government on oil and gas, founded by a controversial Cameroonian businessman, Njock Ayuk Eyong , although he claims to have handed over the firm to younger staff members.
• Anxiety about the sale feeds into a general concern in the South Durban basin amongst environmental activists and academics that Shell and BP will shrug off their role in polluting the communities in which SAPREF has operated since the early 1960s.
• Longstanding community exposure to refinery emissions in South Durban has been found by academics; for example Ecoserv found 124 exceedances of WHO SO₂ guidelines in Merebank (Nov 2000–Oct 2002). Another document logs pollution incidents from 16 Jan 1998 of SAPREF pollution from 16 Jan 1998 – 26 July 2011 (Document DD5 Page 11 – 21 flares, spills, bad smells, toxic chemicals etc)
• Its’ quite hard to show tangible evidence showing a direct link between SAPREF and illness, and easier for academics and activists to talk about studies that have been done.
• Meanwhile a former SAPREF worker, MK Murugan, not 70 years old, who developed toxic hepatitis from working in SAPREF, has spent half his life fighting the company for compensation. His legal battle to get the company to recognise his illness and then pay him compensation highlights the difficulties that impacted communities might have in trying to get compensation and most importantly acknowledgement from SAPREF that they need to improve their safety record going forward. Improving their safety to lessen pollution will make the newly envisaged refinery even more expensive.


Extra Budget Items:
We many need to buy in archive of previous environmental spills and accidents in the Durban South Basin where all the industrial plants are located.

Press Release:


Refinery for a Rand
Why has government bought a broken oil refinery, while global companies simply walk away? It was the country’s largest crude oil refinery, supplying around a third of our fuel, until it was flooded in 2022. Then last year, after Durban’s SAPREF refinery had stood derelict for months, government agreed to buy it for the symbolic sum of R1. Leaked documents raise red flags about the purchase, while activists say the sale allows international oil giants to shirk responsibility for polluting local communities. How was government persuaded into a deal that will commit the country to a fossil fuel future? And who will pay the true price?
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Erin Bates

Script:


(Erin) For how much would you buy this oil refinery, the largest in South Africa?
Would you spend hundreds of millions? Or billions?
The South African Government has just bought it for a single rand, from two global oil giants.

(Michael Marchant) Shell and BP say, no need for the money. We'll take the nominal one rand and we'll walk away.

(Erin) So is this a bargain? Or is it a deal that could leave the taxpayer with heavy clean-up costs?

(Rajen Naidoo) For me, it is a health concern, it's the legacy problem. Who takes care of that community that has been affected?

(Bobby Peek) There is the elite behind government that sees government merely as a money-making machine.

(Erin) Our story starts here on the Kwazulu-Natal coast, in the industrial heartland of eThekwini. Bongani Mthembu works for an anti-pollution NGO. He regularly tests air and water to collect data, in a bid to protect locals from what he calls a toxic soup of often invisible chemical waste. His concerns now take on a new urgency, as the sale of the nearby refinery raises questions about who’s to take responsibility for its toxic legacy.

(Bongani Mthembu) We are always first on scene when incidents and accidents happen, and government come after. We always have to to to be fighting with them to do what they what they're supposed to be doing.

(Erin) The area where Bongani collects his samples has long been the home of heavy industry - oil refineries, factories and industrial plants. But for even longer, it’s been the home of working class communities who breathe in polluted air and deal with industrial incidents: flares, leaks and explosions.

(Bongani Mthembu) This industry, they've there's an historical, environmental and health impact, you know, and they've gotten away with murder, you know, for so many years, disregarding the very same people that you call your neighbours, ja, it’s totally unacceptable.

(Bongani Mthembu): So ja, this is the refinery that was bought for one rand.

(Erin) From the viewpoint, we can see what was historically one of the biggest culprits:
Sapref, the oil refinery which we’ve just bought. It’s had a chequered emissions history, but is no longer operational.

(Erin) SAPREF was built in 1963, that’s more than sixty years ago.
But for the people of Durban South it’s been more neighbour than friend, depending on who you talk to.

(Erin) Sapref was constructed under apartheid by BP and Shell.
For decades its smokestacks belched emissions which mingled with the industrial smog of Durban South. We covered this story as early as 2000, when citizen scientists starting testing the air to confirm their worst suspicions. The community claims irresponsible industries have caused unnaturally high levels of disease - cancer, heart issues and asthma.

(Woman) It’s like your lungs are caving in, your chest is going to just explode.

(Erin) So twenty-five years later, is there still a problem? The Head of Occupational Health at the University of Kwazulu-Natal, Professor Rajen Naidoo, says the impact of pollution lives on.

(Rajen Naidoo) The child who was made sick while the refinery was still operating is going to have to carry that burden through into adulthood. And so the legacy does not stop at the point of you closing your doors.

(Erin) Locals have made it their business to monitor their industrial neighbours. But earlier this year they were shocked to hear that Sapref - now at the end of its life - had been sold, literally behind their backs to the Central Energy Fund, a state-owned enterprise.

(Erin) Are you aware of any community engagement about this acquisition by CEF? Were there any consultations?

(Bongani Mthembu) No

(Erin) You represent or are linked to 21 community organizations in this area?

(Bongani Mthembu) No, public participation on this acquisition, no.

(Erin) And the terms of the sale were even more astonishing, detailed in a bundle of secret documents handed to Michael Marchant who is the senior investigator for Open Secrets, an organisation that probes the links between government and powerful corporates. The leak is a thousand pages, mostly of due diligence reports advising government on the risks attached to the sale.

(Michael Marchant) All of that documentation comes in. In 2021 we have a picture of everything the Central Energy Fund is told to look out for when it comes to the refinery.

(Erin) So the red flags?

(Michael Marchant) All of the red flags, pretty much, are laid out in 2021.

(Erin) Technical reports list all the estimated costs to manage the refinery into the future.

(Michael Marchant) You've got the three billion for basic maintenance, eight billion, maybe even more, for the new fuel requirements, and six billion rand for decommissioning liabilities.

(Erin) But then, in 2022, the negotiations are disrupted by dramatic and deadly floods.
Durban’s cancer valley was deluged.

(Michael Marchant) After the floods in KwaZulu-Natal, the refinery is actually under three meters of water, huge damage, I mean, it's really devastating. You're talking about hydrocarbons being washed out onto the beaches, it makes everything worse and more complicated.

(Erin) Sapref ground to a halt, as did the negotiations around the sale.

(Erin) After the floodwaters had subsided, the government could have insisted BP and Shell clean up the mess.
But instead they returned to the negotiating table and were guided by a new set of documents.

(Erin) In May 2024, Sapref is sold voetstoots. The state buys, for a single rand, a rusting, antiquated refinery, its infrastructure, the land it sits on - and its liabilities.

(Michael Marchant) You have to ask why two large multinational corporations would be willing to walk away from a refinery that they'd owned for nearly 60 years, and I think the extent of how much it's going to cost to fix and rehabilitate is a central part of answering that question.

(Erin) One of the consultancies was CLG, originally founded as the Centurion Law Group by a controversial businessman from Cameroon, NJ Ayuk.
He has been invited into government’s inner circle - and is a cheerleader for fossil fuels.

(NJ Ayuk) There is only one thing I am going to tell you on Shell Drill Baby Drill.

(Erin) In the leaked documents, the whistleblower alleges that CLG played a problematic role in the Sapref deal - which might set the scene for what happened next.

(Erin) In its heyday, Sapref was producing 180-thousand barrels of fuel a day.
This year the government revealed a plan to revamp it into a mega-refinery, producing at least 400-thousand barrels a day in order to meet fuel consumption nationally and to break even.

(Erin) Government now dreams of nearly tripling Sapref’s output. But who will pay - and who will breathe the fumes? That’s the concern of Durban-based environmental activist Bobby Peek, Director of Groundwork.

(Bobby Peek) South Durban communities will not allow it, and Groundwork will stand by them. We will not allow a oil refinery to be built that will have huge implications because who's going to find that money and who's going to float it?

(Erin) Bobby sits on the Presidential Commission for a Just Transition to Renewable Energy because of the work he has done campaigning for clean air and water over decades.
For him, this sale is a betrayal by Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe who insists fossil fuels remain central to energy policy.

(Bobby Peek) That is a sell-out. Gwede has thrown us under the bus. He has hijacked the just transition, and he is going to bring death to the people of South Durban if that refinery starts up again. You speak to people on the streets about the families that suffer with cancer. You know, the children are breathing heavy, you know, in the area because of the sulphur dioxide pollution, which is linked to asthma. And so those are the realities of the area.

(Upsound Voice) Over half the amount of children complaining of burning sensation…

(Erin) Twenty-five years ago we interviewed a refinery worker who showed us a list of the names of dead colleagues.

(Refinery Worker) Those are the names now of my acquaintances and friends, everyone of them was an employee of SAPREF either or Engen and everyone of those names they have passed on with the cancer.

(Erin) Now we have been leaked an even longer list, allegedly showing deaths of Sapref workers due to cancer and heart attacks in that same period. Sapref did not respond to questions to confirm the list - and there’s no public study to refer to.

(Erin) The refinery has been going for over 60 years.

(Rajen Naidoo) That’s right.

(Erin) And not a single study on the worker impact?

(Rajen Naidoo) To the best of my knowledge, there's not been any studies. That's not to say that the data is not there, because, as a working environment, certainly since 1994 when we had the Occupational Health and Safety Act, all companies are expected to have medical surveillance programs so companies ought to have this information about whether workers have been developing any illnesses.

(Erin) Former Sapref employee, Maslamony Kisten Murugan, has told his story of ill-health through the courts. He worked in Sapref from the age of twenty. But from 1996 he was frequently hospitalised with acute stomach pain. Doctors diagnosed him with toxic hepatitis, a sickness of the liver following exposure to chemicals.

(Maslamony Murugan) If you are breathing this carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, sometimes you can lose your breath. It was unbearable.

(Erin) And did it burn your eyes? Did it make -

(Maslamony Murugan) Nose, smoke goes up and it comes down because it's heavier than air. Comes down and when you breathe that you choke. That happens in winter, as the air is little bit heavy and it's cold.

(Upsound Erin) That’s you, at a young age.

(Erin) For decades Maslamony has been fighting with Sapref. He accuses the refinery of reducing his salary when illness undermined his ability to work.

(Maslamony Murugan) It was difficult. I lost two cars. I nearly lose a house. After I was dismissed, I got nothing, and prior to dismissal, they brought my salary down from 17 700 to 5000.

(Erin) So does it come as a surprise that consultants advise the new owners of Sapref to set up a war chest, and to get insurance for what might come? It’s all there in black and white in the leaked documents.

(Michael Marchant) They mention explicitly the risk of community class actions, essentially saying to the Central Energy Fund you have to take into account that should it be shown down the line that the refinery is having these types of impacts, it’s a potentially huge liability that you are taking on. And then what is I guess telling and goes to the centre of this investigation: “We have proposed - and the sellers have rejected that proposal – to include any of these liabilities in the sale and purchase agreement.”

(Erin) So while Government - and by extension the taxpayer - buy a refinery for a single rand, the multi-national oil companies demand and get a clean break from the past.

(Bobby Peek) Somebody walked away with a load of dosh, and that is Shell and BP, because they don't have to clean up, and that is what we call the externalization of pollution. You externalize those costs onto society.

(Erin) Attempts to get comment from all the parties engaged in this sale came to nothing, save for BP which said they were satisfied with the deal

(Bobby Peek) I think, globally, we should go after Shell and BP for walking away, and forcing them in London and in The Hague to pay reparations and to pay for the entire clean-up, every cent of that oil refinery.

(Erin) Officials justify the purchase as fuel security. Critics call it a ticking time bomb of debt and disease. Who is right? And who will carry the burden when generations to come ask why we paid just one rand for a refinery - and so much more for its consequences?

(Michael Marchant) It’s a clean break for Shell and BP, but it's an incredibly dirty deal in terms of the state of South Africa. But of course, it's also an incredibly dirty deal for the communities living around that refinery.

The leak is a thousand pages, mostly of due diligence reports advising government on the risks attached to the sale. (Michael Marchant) All of that documentation comes in. In 2021 we have a picture of everything the Central Energy Fund is told to look out for when it comes to the refinery. (Erin) So the red flags? (Michael Marchant) All of the red flags, pretty much, are laid out in 2021. (Erin) Technical reports list all the estimated costs to manage the refinery into the future. (Michael Marchant) You've got the three billion for basic maintenance, eight billion, maybe even more, for the new fuel requirements, and six billion rand for decommissioning liabilities. (Erin) But then, in 2022, the negotiations are disrupted by dramatic and deadly floods. Durban’s cancer valley was deluged. (Michael Marchant) After the floods in KwaZulu-Natal, the refinery is actually under three meters of water, huge damage, I mean, it's really devastating. You're talking about hydrocarbons being washed out onto the beaches, it makes everything worse and more complicated. (Erin) Sapref ground to a halt, as did the negotiations around the sale. (Erin) After the floodwaters had subsided, the government could have insisted BP and Shell clean up the mess. But instead they returned to the negotiating table and were guided by a new set of documents. (Erin) In May 2024, Sapref is sold voetstoots. The state buys, for a single rand, a rusting, antiquated refinery, its infrastructure, the land it sits on - and its liabilities. (Michael Marchant) You have to ask why two large multinational corporations would be willing to walk away from a refinery that they'd owned for nearly 60 years, and I think the extent of how much it's going to cost to fix and rehabilitate is a central part of answering that question. (Erin) One of the consultancies was CLG, originally founded as the Centurion Law Group by a controversial businessman from Cameroon, NJ Ayuk. He has been invited into government’s inner circle - and is a cheerleader for fossil fuels. (NJ Ayuk) There is only one thing I am going to tell you on Shell Drill Baby Drill. (Erin) In the leaked documents, the whistleblower alleges that CLG played a problematic role in the Sapref deal - which might set the scene for what happened next. (Erin) In its heyday, Sapref was producing 180-thousand barrels of fuel a day. This year the government revealed a plan to revamp it into a mega-refinery, producing at least 400-thousand barrels a day in order to meet fuel consumption nationally and to break even. (Erin) Government now dreams of nearly tripling Sapref’s output. But who will pay - and who will breathe the fumes? That’s the concern of Durban-based environmental activist Bobby Peek, Director of Groundwork. (Bobby Peek) South Durban communities will not allow it, and Groundwork will stand by them. We will not allow a oil refinery to be built that will have huge implications because who's going to find that money and who's going to float it? (Erin) Bobby sits on the Presidential Commission for a Just Transition to Renewable Energy because of the work he has done campaigning for clean air and water over decades. For him, this sale is a betrayal by Energy Minister Gwede Mantashe who insists fossil fuels remain central to energy policy. (Bobby Peek) That is a sell-out. Gwede has thrown us under the bus. He has hijacked the just transition, and he is going to bring death to the people of South Durban if that refinery starts up again. You speak to people on the streets about the families that suffer with cancer. You know, the children are breathing heavy, you know, in the area because of the sulphur dioxide pollution, which is linked to asthma. And so those are the realities of the area. (Upsound Voice) Over half the amount of children complaining of burning sensation… (Erin) Twenty-five years ago we interviewed a refinery worker who showed us a list of the names of dead colleagues. (Refinery Worker) Those are the names now of my acquaintances and friends, everyone of them was an employee of SAPREF either or Engen and everyone of those names they have passed on with the cancer. (Erin) Now we have been leaked an even longer list, allegedly showing deaths of Sapref workers due to cancer and heart attacks in that same period. Sapref did not respond to questions to confirm the list - and there’s no public study to refer to. (Erin) The refinery has been going for over 60 years. (Rajen Naidoo) That’s right. (Erin) And not a single study on the worker impact? (Rajen Naidoo) To the best of my knowledge, there's not been any studies. That's not to say that the data is not there, because, as a working environment, certainly since 1994 when we had the Occupational Health and Safety Act, all companies are expected to have medical surveillance programs so companies ought to have this information about whether workers have been developing any illnesses. (Erin) Former Sapref employee, Maslamony Kisten Murugan, has told his story of ill-health through the courts. He worked in Sapref from the age of twenty. But from 1996 he was frequently hospitalised with acute stomach pain. Doctors diagnosed him with toxic hepatitis, a sickness of the liver following exposure to chemicals. (Maslamony Murugan) If you are breathing this carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, sometimes you can lose your breath. It was unbearable. (Erin) And did it burn your eyes? Did it make - (Maslamony Murugan) Nose, smoke goes up and it comes down because it's heavier than air. Comes down and when you breathe that you choke. That happens in winter, as the air is little bit heavy and it's cold. (Upsound Erin) That’s you, at a young age. (Erin) For decades Maslamony has been fighting with Sapref. He accuses the refinery of reducing his salary when illness undermined his ability to work. (Maslamony Murugan) It was difficult. I lost two cars. I nearly lose a house. After I was dismissed, I got nothing, and prior to dismissal, they brought my salary down from 17 700 to 5000. (Erin) So does it come as a surprise that consultants advise the new owners of Sapref to set up a war chest, and to get insurance for what might come? It’s all there in black and white in the leaked documents. (Michael Marchant) They mention explicitly the risk of community class actions, essentially saying to the Central Energy Fund you have to take into account that should it be shown down the line that the refinery is having these types of impacts, it’s a potentially huge liability that you are taking on. And then what is I guess telling and goes to the centre of this investigation: “We have proposed - and the sellers have rejected that proposal – to include any of these liabilities in the sale and purchase agreement.” (Erin) So while Government - and by extension the taxpayer - buy a refinery for a single rand, the multi-national oil companies demand and get a clean break from the past. (Bobby Peek) Somebody walked away with a load of dosh, and that is Shell and BP, because they don't have to clean up, and that is what we call the externalization of pollution. You externalize those costs onto society. (Erin) Attempts to get comment from all the parties engaged in this sale came to nothing, save for BP which said they were satisfied with the deal (Bobby Peek) I think, globally, we should go after Shell and BP for walking away, and forcing them in London and in The Hague to pay reparations and to pay for the entire clean-up, every cent of that oil refinery. (Erin) Officials justify the purchase as fuel security. Critics call it a ticking time bomb of debt and disease. Who is right? And who will carry the burden when generations to come ask why we paid just one rand for a refinery - and so much more for its consequences? (Michael Marchant) It’s a clean break for Shell and BP, but it's an incredibly dirty deal in terms of the state of South Africa. But of course, it's also an incredibly dirty deal for the communities living around that refinery.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We ask why two global oil companies - BP and Shell - have been able to away from a broken, non-functioning refinery, abandoning their responsibility to the community for decades of pollution, passing
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have access to whistleblower documents which show how consultants shifted their perspective from one year to the next on why selling the SAPREF refinery in Durban was a good idea for government. Those whistleblower documents suggest that behind the wall of silence on the sale in which the state paid a single rand there may have been manipulation to tie South Africa back in to a fossil fuel agenda.
metadata.Summary: • In May 2024, the state-owned Central Energy Fund (CEF) agreed to acquire the SAPREF refinery assets in South Durban from BP and Shell for R1 (symbolic sum), subject to approvals, after it had been flooded in 2022. • A whistle-blower dumped 1000 + pages of documents at OUTA including complicated Due Diligence documents, suggesting that government was taking this decision without proper advice or advice designed to avoid the questions of environmental liability. • Open Secrets then published whistle-blower-backed investigations (July 2025) detailing the R1 sale and the “clean-break/voetstoots” nature of the deal and due-diligence red flags. • One of the red flags is concern about the role of a consulting company Centurion Law Group which has a known poor track record in advising Government on oil and gas, founded by a controversial Cameroonian businessman, Njock Ayuk Eyong , although he claims to have handed over the firm to younger staff members. • Anxiety about the sale feeds into a general concern in the South Durban basin amongst environmental activists and academics that Shell and BP will shrug off their role in polluting the communities in which SAPREF has operated since the early 1960s. • Longstanding community exposure to refinery emissions in South Durban has been found by academics; for example Ecoserv found 124 exceedances of WHO SO₂ guidelines in Merebank (Nov 2000–Oct 2002). Another document logs pollution incidents from 16 Jan 1998 of SAPREF pollution from 16 Jan 1998 – 26 July 2011 (Document DD5 Page 11 – 21 flares, spills, bad smells, toxic chemicals etc) • Its’ quite hard to show tangible evidence showing a direct link between SAPREF and illness, and easier for academics and activists to talk about studies that have been done. • Meanwhile a former SAPREF worker, MK Murugan, not 70 years old, who developed toxic hepatitis from working in SAPREF, has spent half his life fighting the company for compensation. His legal battle to get the company to recognise his illness and then pay him compensation highlights the difficulties that impacted communities might have in trying to get compensation and most importantly acknowledgement from SAPREF that they need to improve their safety record going forward. Improving their safety to lessen pollution will make the newly envisaged refinery even more expensive.
